title: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING FIRST THAT MOST PEOPLE KEEP SKIPPING
paragraphs: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING FIRST THAT MOST PEOPLE KEEP SKIPPING

Everyone wants the freedom Jesus promised in John 8:32. But the words immediately before that promise reveal why so many people know the truth, quote the truth, defend the truth… and still live like prisoners.
There is a kind of prison you can walk out of every morning without anyone noticing.
You can go to work from it. Raise children in it. Lead worship in it. Preach sermons in it. Post Bible verses from it. Smile for photographs while its invisible walls are closing in around your soul.
And the frightening thing?
You can become so accustomed to those walls that you eventually stop calling them a prison.
You call them your personality.
Your past.
Your weakness.
Your circumstances.
You tell yourself, "This is just who I am."
But what if the thing you have learned to live with is the very thing Jesus came to set you free from?
What if you have been quoting the promise of freedom while quietly ignoring the invitation that comes before it?
Because Jesus never simply said, "The truth will set you free," as though truth were some inspirational statement you could hang on your wall and forget by Monday morning.
He said something first.
Something that changes everything.
And once you see it, you may never read John 8:32 the same way again.
In John 8:31–32, Jesus spoke these words to Jews who had believed Him:
"If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." (John 8:31–32, KJV)
Read that again.
Not just the beautiful ending.
The beginning.
"If ye continue in my word…"
There is an invitation before the promise.
There is discipleship before the declaration of freedom.
There is a relationship with Christ that cannot be reduced to agreeing with a few religious statements.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us want Jesus to remove the chains while we keep holding on to the things that helped forge them.
We want peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without confession.
Transformation without repentance.
Freedom without allowing His Word to confront what is destroying us.
We want the comfort of His promises while resisting the authority of His voice.
And somehow, when the same wounds keep reopening and the same sins keep returning, we wonder why the truth we have heard so many times has not changed the way we live.
But Jesus was not offering a motivational slogan.
He was calling people to become His disciples.
And His words were far more searching than we sometimes realize.
In the original Greek, John 8:31 reads:
Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ, ἀληθῶς μαθηταί μού ἐστε.
Ean hymeis meinēte en tō logō tō emō, alēthōs mathētai mou este.
"If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples."
The word μείνητε (meinēte) comes from the Greek verb μένω (menō), meaning to remain, stay, continue, or abide.
Jesus was not describing a passing emotional experience.
He was describing a continuing relationship with His teaching.
Not a moment of inspiration followed by a lifetime of indifference.
Not one Sunday of conviction followed by six days of deliberately silencing His voice.
Not perfect performance, either.
Because abiding is not the same as never stumbling.
It is continuing with Christ rather than abandoning Him.
It is returning to His Word when your feelings want to lead you elsewhere.
It is allowing His teaching to correct you when correction is uncomfortable.
It is staying near enough to hear Him even when what He says exposes something you would rather hide.
And perhaps that is the part that hurts.
Because we love the Jesus who comforts us.
But do we love Him enough to listen when He corrects us?
We love hearing that He forgives.
But will we listen when He tells us to forgive?
We love hearing that He is faithful.
But will we trust Him when obedience becomes costly?
We love proclaiming that He is Lord.
But what happens when His Word contradicts the life we have been defending?
That is where the question becomes unavoidable.
Are we following Jesus?
Or have we become comfortable following our own preferences while asking Jesus to bless the journey?
There is a difference.
And that difference matters eternally.
Notice something else in the passage.
Jesus was speaking to people who had believed Him.
Yet, as the conversation continues, some of His hearers resist His words with increasing hostility. By John 8:59, the scene has become deeply confrontational.
That context matters.
Jesus was exposing the difference between an initial favorable response to His message and the genuine discipleship that continues in His Word.
He was not teaching that we purchase salvation through religious effort.
Scripture is clear:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV)
Salvation is God's gift.
We cannot earn it by reading enough chapters, attending enough services, donating enough money, or collecting enough good deeds.
But the grace that saves us does not leave us content to remain enslaved to the very sins from which Christ came to redeem us.
Jesus does not demand that we clean ourselves up before we come to Him.
He calls us to come to Him, and His grace begins changing us.
That is the difference between trying to earn His love and learning to live in His love.
One produces exhausted religious performance.
The other produces grateful obedience.
And if you have ever been exhausted from trying to appear spiritually strong while secretly falling apart, you need to hear this.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend that you are free. He is calling you to bring your chains into His light.
Maybe your prison is bitterness.
Someone hurt you years ago, and although the conversation ended, the argument has continued inside your mind ever since.
You replay what they said.
You imagine what you should have said.
You carry their offense into relationships with people who never wounded you.
And whenever the Holy Spirit brings forgiveness to your attention, you remember how much they hurt you.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil was acceptable. It does not require returning to an unsafe relationship or abandoning wise boundaries.
But it does mean refusing to make revenge the ruler of your heart.
Maybe your prison is a secret sin.
You have promised God so many times that you would stop.
You meant it every time.
You cried.
You prayed.
You deleted things.
You made new rules.
And then, in a moment of loneliness, anger, exhaustion, or temptation, you returned to what you swore you were leaving behind.
Now you are afraid to pray because you feel like a hypocrite.
You wonder whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
You wonder whether someone like you can really change.
Or perhaps your prison is not something outwardly scandalous at all.
Maybe it is pride.
The kind that never admits wrongdoing.
The kind that can explain everyone else's sins but refuses to examine its own.
The kind that uses Bible verses to win arguments while avoiding the verses that expose the heart.
Maybe it is fear.
Maybe it is the need to be admired.
Maybe it is the belief that your worth depends on being needed, noticed, attractive, successful, or spiritually impressive.
Maybe you are not running toward some obvious temptation.
Maybe you are running from silence because silence forces you to face the condition of your soul.
And Jesus sees it.
Not merely the polished version people applaud.
Not merely the photographs, testimonies, ministry activities, and religious vocabulary.
He sees the exhausted person behind all of it.
The one who knows exactly what to say when someone asks, "How are you?"
"I'm blessed."
"I'm okay."
"God is good."
And God is good.
But sometimes you are not okay.
Sometimes you are wounded.
Sometimes you are hiding.
Sometimes you are carrying something that needs to be confessed, confronted, grieved, or surrendered.
And the tragedy is not that Jesus knows.
The tragedy is that you may be afraid to let Him deal with what He already sees.
Listen carefully to the next words of Jesus.
In John 8:32, the Greek says:
καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.
Kai gnōsesthe tēn alētheian, kai hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas.
"And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
The Greek word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
The verb ἐλευθερώσει (eleutherōsei) means "will set free" or "will liberate."
But here is something we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus does not leave the meaning of this freedom to our imagination.
His hearers respond by appealing to their descent from Abraham and questioning why they would need to be made free.
Jesus answers in John 8:34:
"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." (KJV)
The Greek expression is even more revealing:
δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας
Doulos estin tēs hamartias.
"He is a slave of sin."
The word doulos refers to a slave, someone under another's mastery.
Jesus was speaking about bondage to sin.
Not merely difficult circumstances.
Not simply the freedom to express ourselves.
Not the modern idea that freedom means doing whatever we want without anyone telling us otherwise.
Because sometimes doing whatever we want is exactly how our bondage reveals itself.
We say, "Nobody controls me."
But anger controls our reactions.
Lust controls our attention.
Pride controls our apologies.
Envy controls our contentment.
Fear controls our decisions.
And the approval of other people controls the version of ourselves we allow the world to see.
We call it independence.
Jesus calls us to recognize the slavery underneath.
And then comes one of the most beautiful declarations in the entire chapter.
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." (John 8:36, KJV)
There it is.
The center of everything.
Not simply truth as an abstract principle.
Not biblical knowledge detached from the Savior.
Not self-improvement disguised as Christianity.
The Son.
Jesus Christ.
The One who does not merely describe freedom but has the authority to give it.
This is why we must never separate John 8:32 from John 8:36.
The truth that sets us free is inseparable from the Son who sets us free.
Later, Jesus declares:
"I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." (John 14:6, KJV)
The One who calls us to abide in His Word is Himself the truth.
And that changes the entire picture.
Christian freedom is not merely learning enough information to become a better person.
It is being brought into a saving relationship with Jesus Christ, who delivers sinners from the dominion of sin and calls them into a new life.
Think about that.
The Savior who knows everything about you is the same Savior who willingly went to the cross for sinners.
He knew what humanity would do.
He knew betrayal.
He knew denial.
He knew hatred.
He knew the depth of human rebellion.
And still, He went to Calvary.
Not because sin was small.
But because His love was great.
At the cross, God's holiness was not ignored.
Sin was not excused.
Justice was not dismissed.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for our sins.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares, so that we might die to sins and live unto righteousness.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we were good enough to deserve rescue.
But that Christ came to save sinners.
Not that our past was imaginary.
But that His grace is greater than our guilt.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that His mercy makes repentance a doorway back to the God we have sinned against.
And now the invitation becomes personal.
Because the same Jesus who spoke in John 8 is not asking you to admire freedom from a distance.
He is calling you to follow Him.
To remain in His Word.
To trust Him.
To turn from sin.
To stop making peace with what is destroying your soul.
To stop treating conviction as an enemy when it may be the very mercy that brings you back to Him.
And no, that does not mean the Christian life becomes instantly painless.
Some habits require sustained struggle.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, and healing.
Some relationships need boundaries.
Some consequences remain even after forgiveness.
And believers still face temptation and must continue depending on God's grace.
But freedom in Christ means sin no longer has the rightful claim to rule those who belong to Him.
Romans 6:14 says:
"For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace."
That is not permission to continue sinning without concern.
Paul immediately rejects that misunderstanding.
It is a declaration that grace brings us under a new Master.
And His name is Jesus.
Perhaps you have fallen again.
Perhaps this week you said something cruel.
Perhaps you returned to a habit you had been fighting.
Perhaps you have been living a double life, outwardly devoted but inwardly distant.
Perhaps you have been angry at God because life has not unfolded the way you prayed it would.
And now, reading these words, you feel that familiar heaviness.
Shame.
Regret.
Fear.
The thought that whispers, "You have failed too many times."
But hear what Scripture says.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:9, KJV)
Not because confession magically earns forgiveness.
But because God is faithful, and the cleansing He provides rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not need to defend your sin before the One who died to save you from it.
You do not need to pretend the wound is healed before asking Him for help.
You do not need to manufacture spiritual strength to make yourself worthy of His mercy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting Christ.
And keep coming to His Word.
Even when it corrects you.
Especially when it corrects you.
Because the Word of God is not merely something to consult when life falls apart.
It is the truth by which we learn to live.
When bitterness rises, return to His Word.
When temptation whispers, return to His Word.
When the enemy accuses, remember what His Word says about the finished work of Christ.
When pride makes you unwilling to apologize, return to His Word.
When fear tells you that obedience will cost too much, remember the Savior who gave everything to redeem you.
Not as a religious ritual to earn His approval.
But as a disciple learning to remain in the voice of the Shepherd.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." (KJV)
There is that language again.
Abiding.
Remaining.
Continuing.
Life flowing from a relationship with Christ.
A branch does not produce fruit by pretending to be alive.
It bears fruit because it remains connected to the vine.
And perhaps this is what your soul has been missing.
Not another emotional high.
Not another inspirational quote.
Not another temporary promise to become better through willpower alone.
But a deeper, daily dependence upon Jesus Christ.
His Word shaping your thoughts.
His grace teaching you to say no to ungodliness.
His Spirit producing fruit that your own strength could never manufacture.
His forgiveness lifting the burden of confessed sin.
His truth confronting the lies you have believed for years.
This is where freedom begins to become visible in ordinary life.
When you finally admit you were wrong instead of protecting your pride.
When you refuse to feed a secret temptation.
When you seek help instead of hiding.
When you forgive without pretending the wound never happened.
When you open Scripture even though your emotions feel numb.
When you choose obedience while your feelings are still catching up.
When you stop asking, "How close can I get to sin without falling?"
And begin asking, "Lord Jesus, how can I walk closer to You?"
Not perfection overnight.
But real repentance.
Real faith.
Real growth.
Real grace.
And a real Savior who does not abandon His people.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always been so much more than an inspirational phrase.
Consider Peter.
He confidently declared that he was ready to die with Jesus.
Then, in the courtyard, fear overtook his courage.
Three times he denied knowing his Lord.
And the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered His words.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that moment?
The sound of the rooster.
The weight of what he had done.
The realization that the mouth which had promised loyalty had spoken denial.
For Peter, it was not an abstract theological discussion.
It was personal failure.
Public weakness.
A terrible collapse at the very moment he wanted to be brave.
But that was not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the care of His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
Peter's denial was real.
His tears were real.
His restoration was real.
And the grace of Christ was greater than his failure.
That is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is reason never to treat the mercy of Jesus as though it were too small to redeem a repentant sinner.
Perhaps you see yourself in Peter.
You promised loyalty.
Then pressure came.
Fear came.
Temptation came.
And you discovered how weak you could be.
But your failure does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
Jesus Christ is still the Savior of sinners.
And if you belong to Him, His Word is not calling you into hopeless condemnation.
It is calling you back to the truth.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the One who alone can make you free.
I want to ask you something now.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not to embarrass you.
But because some questions deserve more than a quick answer.
What is the one area of your life where you keep asking God for freedom while resisting what His Word has already told you?
You do not have to announce every private struggle publicly.
Some confessions belong in prayer, and some need to be shared with a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, counselor, or person who can help you walk toward healing and accountability.
But do not let secrecy become your hiding place.
If Christ has already brought you through a season of bondage, consider sharing a testimony of His grace. Your story may help another believer realize that repentance and restoration are possible.
And if you are not ready to share anything publicly, that is okay too.
The most important response is not the comment people see.
It is the honest response you make before God.
Not because saving a post makes you more spiritual.

But because there may come a night when temptation feels louder than conviction, when shame tells you to hide, or when you need to remember the difference between knowing a Bible verse and abiding in the Savior who spoke it.
Return to John 8:31–36.
Read it slowly.
Read the whole conversation.
Let Jesus define the freedom He promises.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Maybe a family member who has grown distant from faith.
A friend quietly struggling with addiction or shame.
A believer exhausted from trying to maintain appearances.
Someone who knows the language of Christianity but has lost the joy of walking with Christ.
Not everyone who needs the Gospel will walk into a church this week.
Some may encounter a biblical truth while scrolling through their phone after a difficult day.
Some may begin asking questions they have avoided for years.
And some may be reminded that the door of repentance is not closed to those who turn to Christ.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus through Scripture, biblical conviction, encouragement, repentance, forgiveness, healing, and discipleship.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to walk alongside this mission.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not have the means to purchase books or other learning materials.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry like this requires real work, time, and resources.
Writing, preparing, organizing, and distributing discipleship materials takes continued effort.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not make you more loved by Jesus.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you already have to your family, your local church, or those in genuine need.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that helps support the ongoing work of this ministry.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that generosity should be willing rather than pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
If you choose to direct part of your voluntary ministry-giving budget toward Gospel Warrior, we would be grateful for that support.
Not because God needs your money.
But because ministries use earthly resources to carry out real work, and willing supporters can help make that work possible.
These items are simply resources and expressions of encouragement. They are not spiritual necessities, and purchasing them does not bring anyone closer to salvation.
The greatest gift we can ever point you toward is not something we sell.
It is the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
You can still read, pray, learn, share, invite others, and make use of our free discipleship resources.
A sincere prayer matters.
A thoughtful conversation matters.
A shared Scripture can matter.
And no financial circumstance can diminish your worth before God.
What matters most is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are encouraged to know Him, trust Him, and follow His Word.
Because this was never supposed to be about building a platform that points people toward us.
It is about serving a mission that points people toward Him.
And that brings us back to the words we began with.
"If ye continue in my word…"
Perhaps you came here because you wanted to feel encouraged.
Perhaps you expected another familiar reminder that the truth would set you free.
But now you have heard the invitation that comes before the promise.
Remain.
Continue.
Abide.
Not in your own righteousness.
Not in your religious reputation.
Not in the illusion that you can save yourself through determination.
Abide in the Word of Jesus Christ.
When you are strong, remain.
When you are weak, remain.
When you understand, remain.
When you are confused, keep bringing your questions to Him.
When you fall, repent and return.
When the world offers you a thousand different versions of freedom, remember the One who said that everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.
And remember what He said next.
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."
There is no greater freedom than being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
No deeper cleansing than the forgiveness He provides.
No more enduring hope than the resurrection of the Savior who conquered death.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every word.
You cannot erase every consequence.
You cannot make your history disappear.
But by God's grace, your history does not have to remain the master of your future.
The same Christ who restored Peter still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The same Christ who died for the ungodly still offers forgiveness through His finished work.
The same Christ who declared that the truth would set His disciples free still calls people to remain in His Word.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, open your Bible.
Begin with John 8.
Read beyond the verse you already know.
And ask Him, sincerely:

"Lord Jesus, show me where I have been hearing Your Word without obeying it. Expose what I have been hiding. Forgive what I have been defending. Teach me to trust Your grace, turn from my sin, and remain in Your truth. I cannot save myself. I need You. Lead me into the freedom that only You can give. Amen."
And when you close your Bible, do not leave His words behind.
Carry them into the apology you need to make.
The temptation you need to resist.
The help you need to seek.
The person you need to forgive.
The truth you need to believe.
The ordinary, unseen decisions in which discipleship becomes more than something you say.
Because the promise was never that a beautiful quotation would break every chain.
The promise was spoken by a living Savior who calls us to abide in His Word.
And the Son is able to make us free indeed.
The prison may have taught you how to survive in chains, but Jesus did not give His life so you would mistake those chains for home.
